text.tspan: Everyday English - C2 - 2026/11/04 - 01 - Essay
People exchange their views in a conversation.
Pexels · 9811867
A conversation worth having
To listen to a friend is to negotiate a familiar but frequently obscured relationship between intentional design and the contingencies of shared experience.
The question is not whether arrangements are desirable, but what authority they should acquire. A credible position supports preparation while withholding
the assumption that procedural coherence is equivalent to human value.
There is a substantive case for structure: asking an open question gives the other person room to explain. Here, we ask what happened instead of
guessing why our friend is upset. The arrangement earns its legitimacy through the specific difficulty it alleviates, not through its conformity to an abstract
ideal of order. Its success is consequently conditional. Once the intervention demands more attention than the obstacle it removes, the original justification
begins to unravel.
An assessment confined to that practical benefit would nevertheless be incomplete, since checking our understanding prevents unnecessary
disagreement. In concrete terms, we repeat the main point in our own words before offering advice. This introduces a problem of perspective: whose
convenience supplies the standard against which improvement is measured? An apparently neutral procedure may privilege the preferences of its
designer. Attentiveness to others makes that asymmetry visible and creates grounds for revision.
What emerges is a qualified defence of planning, rather than a celebration of either control or spontaneity. Arrangements can sustain an experience
without exhausting its meaning. Their authority should remain answerable to the people and circumstances they affect; otherwise, a means of making life
more habitable risks becoming the criterion to which life must conform.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a focused main idea. Develop one supporting reason in each body paragraph, with a concrete example. Conclude by
connecting the two reasons without introducing a new argument. Use the structure as a model; write about an experience of your own.
Explain the meaning before looking at the model answer. What two reasons support the main idea? Explain one example. (Model: The two reasons are
that asking an open question gives the other person room to explain and that checking our understanding prevents unnecessary disagreement. One
example is that we ask what happened instead of guessing why our friend is upset.)
